title: Flexible cystoscopy (and stent removal)
subtitle: Systematic look at the whole bladder under local anaesthetic, with retroflexion

sources.title: EAU Guidelines on Non-muscle-invasive Bladder Cancer
BAUS procedure-specific patient information and consent guidance

indications: Lower urinary tract symptoms where the urethra or bladder must be seen.
contraindications: Acute urinary retention or a stricture that the flexible scope cannot pass (needs a different plan).
preparation: Urine dip or culture; treat infection first.
Check anticoagulants (usually continued for a diagnostic look).
Consent: discomfort, bleeding, infection, and a possible later biopsy.
positioning: Supine (men) or frog-leg (women), the genitalia exposed, a screen so the patient can watch if wished.
equipment: Flexible cystoscope with camera stack, sterile water or saline irrigation, lidocaine gel, graspers for stents, specimen pots.
anatomy: Urethra (meatus, penile, bulbar, membranous, prostatic), verumontanum, bladder neck, trigone, ureteric orifices, dome and anterior wall.
criticalSafety: Look at every part of the bladder, including the anterior wall and the bladder neck in retroflexion.
Stent removal is matched to the stent register.
commonErrors: Missing the anterior wall or the area behind the bladder neck.
Forcing the scope through a stricture.
complications: Dysuria for a day or two.
postop: Drink more for 24 hours; return for fever, rigors or retention.
Results and the next step discussed before the patient leaves.

steps.emphasis: Usually no antibiotic for a diagnostic look; give one only for risk factors or stent removal per local policy.
Supine for men; frog-leg or lithotomy for women; a screen for the patient to watch.
Clean the meatus and glans or vulva; a fenestrated drape.
Pass the flexible scope under vision along the urethra, then map the bladder wall in order.
Explain the findings, document the bladder map, and book any biopsy or TURBT.

step.fcs.la-gel.title: Lidocaine gel and gentle urethral entry
step.fcs.la-gel.why: Gel left in place for a few minutes makes the look painless and lubricates the scope, so the patient stays still and the urethra is not damaged.
how: Instil sterile lidocaine gel into the urethra and wait about 3 to 5 minutes.
Hold the penis upright and stretched (men) and advance the scope only where the lumen is seen ahead.
Ask the patient to breathe out or try to pass urine as the scope reaches the external sphincter.
pitfalls: Starting before the gel has worked.

step.fcs.retroflex.title: Retroflexion to see the bladder neck
step.fcs.retroflex.why: Tumours at the bladder neck and around the internal opening are hidden from the straight view; retroflexion shows them.
how: In the bladder with moderate filling, deflect the tip fully so the scope looks back at its own entry point.
Rotate the scope through 360 degrees to inspect the whole bladder neck and the area around it.
Straighten the tip before withdrawing the scope.
pitfalls: Withdrawing the scope while it is still retroflexed.

step.fcs.stent-removal.title: Stent removal with graspers
step.fcs.stent-removal.why: A stent left in too long encrusts and can block or break. Removing it and closing the register entry ends that risk.
how: Identify the stent coming out of the ureteric orifice.
Pass graspers down the working channel, grasp the stent end and withdraw the scope and stent together.
Check the stent is complete and mark it removed in the stent register.
pitfalls: Pulling only part of an encrusted stent.

step.fcs.finding.title: A suspicious finding
step.fcs.finding.why: A flexible look is for diagnosis. A tumour needs resection under anaesthetic for staging, not a clinic biopsy that loses the muscle layer.
how: Record the site, size, number and appearance of any lesion on a bladder diagram, with photographs.
Explain the finding to the patient and book a TURBT and staging scans as indicated.
Send urine cytology if the bladder looks red or flat-abnormal (possible carcinoma in situ).
pitfalls: Taking a small cold-cup biopsy and calling it staged.
